opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at first it was a bit of a shock. I did my PhD at Maryland in the early 2010s, and my training was very much in the classical tradition: graph-based methods, optimization, sparse representations, carefully designed features. You spent a lot of time thinking about the right mathematical formulation for a problem, and that felt like the core of being a computer vision researcher.

Then around 2012, with the ImageNet results, things started to shift. In the beginning many of us in the traditional camp were skeptical. The models looked like black boxes, the theory wasn't there, and it was hard to accept that a network trained on lots of data could beat methods people had refined for years. But the results kept coming, on one benchmark after another, and at some point you have to be honest with yourself. The evidence was overwhelming.

So my response was to retrain myself. After graduating I was at an industrial research lab, and I spent a lot of time learning the new tools: reading the papers, writing the code, running experiments, basically being a student again. That was humbling, because some of the skills I had worked hard to build suddenly weren't the most valuable thing anymore.

But I also found that the classical training wasn't wasted. Understanding optimization, probabilistic modeling, and how images are formed gave me intuition about why certain architectures or losses might work. When I later moved into generative models, GANs and image-to-image translation, a lot of that older way of thinking about structure and correspondence came back in a new form.

The bigger lesson for me was about attitude. In research, the field can change under your feet very quickly. If you hold on too tightly to what you already know, you get left behind. You have to be willing to let go, follow where the evidence points, and keep learning. I've tried to carry that mindset forward, because I don't think deep learning was the last big shift we'll see.

r001.rationale: He says he retrained by learning deep-learning tools and that researchers must keep learning, but he does not say he developed a habit of learning broadly because he felt nothing in computer vision worked.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest turn as Ming-Yu Liu, drawing only on the conversation given.

To be honest, the first reaction was a bit of fear. I did my PhD at Maryland on fairly classical computer vision, things like hand-designed features, graphical models, carefully engineered pipelines. That was what I'd been trained to do, and I was decent at it. Then around 2012, when AlexNet came out, you could feel the ground shifting. Within a couple of years, the stuff I had spent years learning was simply not competitive anymore.

I think a lot of people in my generation faced the same choice. You could keep defending the old tools and argue that deep learning was a black box, or you could admit that the results spoke for themselves and go learn it. I chose the second path, but it wasn't comfortable. It felt like starting over as a student while already being a researcher at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs. I spent nights reading papers, writing code from scratch, trying to build intuition for why these networks behaved the way they did.

What helped me was realizing that my classical background wasn't wasted. Understanding geometry, probabilistic modeling, and what makes a vision problem hard gave me a way to think about which problems were worth attacking with these new tools. When I later moved to NVIDIA and started working on generative models, image-to-image translation, GANs, that older training shaped how I framed things, even if the techniques were completely different.

So I'd say the response was: accept quickly that the field had changed, be willing to feel like a beginner again, and look for the places where what you already know still gives you an edge. In research, your tools will become obsolete more than once. The habit of relearning is the thing that actually lasts.

r001.rationale: He describes learning deep learning and developing a habit of relearning as the field changed, but does not say he learned broadly because he felt nothing in computer vision worked.

astra-6.text:
I had to be willing to become a beginner again. My training had taught me to think carefully about features, models, and optimization, and suddenly deep learning was changing how those pieces fit together. It was uncomfortable, but I wanted to understand why it worked rather than defend the approach I already knew.

So I started learning and experimenting. I didn’t think of my computer-vision background as something to throw away—it still helped me understand the problems and evaluate the results. But I had to separate that foundation from my attachment to particular methods. The goal was to solve the problem, and if a new approach could do that better, I needed to learn it.

r001.rationale: He says he started learning and experimenting, but does not describe a habit of learning broadly or say he felt that nothing in computer vision worked.

sol-6.1.text:
At first, I was skeptical. My training was in traditional computer vision, where we put a lot of effort into designing features and building models around our understanding of a problem. Deep learning suggested that you could learn much of that directly from data, so it challenged the way I had learned to do research.

But as the results became stronger, I felt I needed to understand it myself. I started learning the methods and experimenting with them. The important shift was becoming willing to be a beginner again. My previous training was still useful, but I couldn’t let the time I had invested in it determine what I worked on next.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he began learning and experimenting with deep learning, but does not describe developing a habit of learning broadly or feeling that nothing in computer vision worked.
